nary_nodes.label: Astronomers announce 'black hole star' discovery
evidence: Astronomers announced Wednesday they had discovered a new type of astronomical object called a "black hole star," potentially solving a mystery involving strange red dots spotted in the early universe.

nary_nodes.label: 'Black hole star' solves red dots mystery
evidence: Astronomers announced Wednesday they had discovered a new type of astronomical object called a "black hole star," potentially solving a mystery involving strange red dots spotted in the early universe.

nary_nodes.label: 'Black hole star' spotted by team
evidence: The black hole star, which dates from 660 million years after the Big Bang, was spotted by a U.S.-led team of astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope, according to a study published Wednesday in the journal Nature.

nary_nodes.label: JWST went online
evidence: Since history's most powerful telescope went online in 2022, it has been spotting many extremely bright cosmic objects dubbed "little red dots" in the early universe that have baffled scientists.

nary_nodes.label: JWST spotting bright cosmic objects
evidence: Since history's most powerful telescope went online in 2022, it has been spotting many extremely bright cosmic objects dubbed "little red dots" in the early universe that have baffled scientists.

nary_nodes.label: Objects' nature debated in JWST era
evidence: "What exactly these objects are has been one of the most debated topics of the JWST era," lead study author Rohan Naidu of the University of Hawaii said in a statement.

nary_nodes.label: Team sought clues for galaxy mystery
evidence: The team had been trying to find clues for a different mystery: why JWST keeps finding bright galaxies in the universe's infancy, when it was thought to have been too early for them to have become so huge.

nary_nodes.label: Red objects assumed surrounded by dust
evidence: "When we see something very red in the universe, we often assume that it is surrounded by dust, like soot or ash," said Robert Simcoe, a study co-author from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

nary_nodes.label: Astronomical objects appear redder through dust
evidence: "The same way that the wildfire smoke from Canada recently made the sky in Boston look bright red, astronomical objects can also appear redder than their intrinsic color when you see them through a veil of dust," he added.

nary_nodes.label: Team sifted through data
evidence: However, when the team sifted through their data, they found that at certain wavelengths, the object's light simply disappeared.

nary_nodes.label: Object's light disappeared at wavelengths
evidence: However, when the team sifted through their data, they found that at certain wavelengths, the object's light simply disappeared.

nary_nodes.label: Object's redness due to hydrogen gas
evidence: To their surprise, this suggested that it is not dust making this object appear red — it is hydrogen gas.

nary_nodes.label: Object not powered by nuclear fusion
evidence: "You can't be powering this by nuclear fusion, which is the energy source that sits at the heart of all the stars," Naidu explained.

nary_nodes.label: Team determined power source scenario
evidence: Using modeling simulations, they determined the most likely scenario was that the object is powered by a central black hole surrounded by a cocoon of gas that makes it resemble a star.

nary_nodes.label: Object powered by central black hole
evidence: Using modeling simulations, they determined the most likely scenario was that the object is powered by a central black hole surrounded by a cocoon of gas that makes it resemble a star.

nary_nodes.label: Team named object MoM-BH*-1
evidence: The team named the object MoM-BH*-1.

nary_nodes.label: Every red dot is a black hole star
evidence: "Every little red dot is consistent with being a black hole star," Naidu said.

nary_nodes.label: MoM-BH*-1 outshines host galaxy
evidence: "What is special about MoM-BH*-1 is, the black hole star is essentially completely outshining its surrounding host galaxy, such that we're seeing pure black hole star light."

nary_nodes.label: Astronomers announce Webb revealed dust/water
evidence: Separately, a team of astronomers announced on Tuesday that the Webb telescope revealed dust and water surviving in the extreme environment of a star located near the Milky Way's central black hole.

nary_nodes.label: Webb revealed dust and water
evidence: Separately, a team of astronomers announced on Tuesday that the Webb telescope revealed dust and water surviving in the extreme environment of a star located near the Milky Way's central black hole.
Webb’s mid-infrared data revealed the clear signature of oxygen-rich silicate dust, as well as, for the first time, water, in IRS 3’s dust envelope.

nary_nodes.label: Observations provide detailed view of IRS 3
evidence: Scientists say the new observations provide the most detailed mid-infrared view yet of the star IRS 3, which is located just 0.55 light-years from Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way galaxy's central supermassive black hole.

nary_nodes.label: Research team identified dust and water
evidence: By analyzing the star's infrared light with the Webb telescope, the research team identified signs of oxygen-rich dust and, for the first time, detected water in the star's surrounding envelope.

nary_nodes.label: Evolved stars produce dust/materials for future stars
evidence: The results show that evolved stars like IRS 3 can still produce dust and other materials important for the creation of future stars – even under the harsh conditions near a supermassive black hole.
Even under the harsh conditions of its environment, stars can produce dust, which will help create future generations of stars!

nary_nodes.label: Galactic centers are extreme environments
evidence: "Galactic centers are among the most extreme environments, so understanding whether stars can continue enriching their surroundings there is an important question," said lead author Florian Peißker of the University of Cologne in Germany.

nary_nodes.label: Understanding star enrichment is important
evidence: "Galactic centers are among the most extreme environments, so understanding whether stars can continue enriching their surroundings there is an important question," said lead author Florian Peißker of the University of Cologne in Germany.

nary_nodes.label: Webb observes resilient dust production
evidence: "With Webb, we can directly observe how stars behave under these conditions and see that dust production remains remarkably resilient."
